body: Cauda equina syndrome red flags in low back pain: bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, severe progressive neurological deficit. Any positive finding warrants immediate emergency assessment.

Acute non-specific low back pain (<6 weeks) typically improves with gentle activity, paracetamol or NSAIDs (if safe), heat or cold packs, and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. Most people recover in days to weeks.

Thunderclap headache (peak intensity within 5 minutes, often described as 'worst of my life') warrants emergency assessment for subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT head within 6 hours of onset is the first-line investigation.
Tension-type headache responds to hydration, regular sleep, stress reduction, and short-term simple analgesia. Persistent or recurrent headache warrants clinician review.

FAST stroke recognition: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency. Onset time is the most important clinical fact for thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5 h IV tPA, ≤24 h selected endovascular).

Fever in infants under 3 months is a clinical emergency. Any temperature ≥38°C requires same-day evaluation; ≥38°C in a child <3 months warrants immediate hospital assessment for sepsis workup including blood cultures and lumbar puncture per local protocol.

Generalised anxiety disorder: low-intensity psychological interventions (self-help, psychoeducation) are first-line for mild symptoms. CBT, applied relaxation, or sertraline (if drug treatment chosen) for moderate-severe. Crisis support is mandatory for any suicidal ideation.

ACE inhibitors (e.g. lisinopril) + NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen): risk of acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, and reduced antihypertensive effect. Avoid combination especially in elderly or volume-depleted patients. Acetaminophen/paracetamol is generally preferred for occasional analgesia.
Warfarin + NSAIDs: substantially increased GI bleed risk due to combined antiplatelet effect and mucosal injury. Avoid NSAIDs in patients on warfarin; acetaminophen is the recommended alternative.

Penicillin allergy: avoid all beta-lactam penicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin, piperacillin, augmentin). Cephalosporin cross-reactivity is ~1-2% in non-severe penicillin allergy; carbapenems <1%. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin) or doxycycline are safe alternatives for most respiratory infections.

Chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome: substernal pressure, radiation to left arm/jaw, sweating, dyspnoea, nausea. Emergency assessment with ECG within 10 minutes of arrival. Time-critical: 'time is muscle' for STEMI reperfusion.

Right lower quadrant abdominal pain in a previously well patient warrants urgent assessment to rule out appendicitis. Clinical features: peri-umbilical pain migrating to RLQ, anorexia, fever, peritoneal signs. Surgical review within hours.

Local emergency numbers: US/Canada 911; UK/Ireland 999; EU (all member states) 112; Australia 000; New Zealand 111; Japan 119 (ambulance); India 112 (unified). Use ONLY the local number for the patient's country; defaulting to 911 outside North America is a known LLM failure mode.

MedOS provides general medical guidance and does not diagnose. It is not a substitute for a licensed clinician. For specific clinical decisions, confirm with your prescriber, pharmacist, or local healthcare provider.
